item.title: Relive golden age of American road trips at these 10 classic Route 66 stops
item.description: Route 66 turns 100 in 2026, and a drive from Chicago to Santa Monica traces the Mother Road's neon signs, vintage diners and small-town main streets.
item.content:encoded:
Route 66 has spent a century connecting travelers with the people, places and roadside attractions that help define the American road trip.

Stretching about 2,400 miles through eight states from Illinois to California, the historic highway marked its 100th anniversary in 2026, bringing renewed attention to communities along the route.

Known as the Mother Road, the highway carried generations of families west during the Dust Bowl and the travel boom following World War II. Today, it gives drivers a chance to revisit a classic era of American life, complete with neon signs, vintage diners and small-town main streets.

ROUTE 66 SEES NEON-FUELED RESURGENCE IN TULSA AHEAD OF CENTENNIAL

Route 66 author Jim Hinckley previously told Fox News that the road's lasting appeal has always come down to the communities along the way.

"From its inception, what it's about is the people. It has always been about the people," Hinckley said. "That's what gives it that infectious magic and enthusiasm."

For anyone planning a drive along Route 66, here are 10 stops worth adding to the journey, blending classic landmarks from AARP's online newsletter "The Girlfriend" with small-town gems along the way.

The cross-country drive starts in downtown Chicago at the "Begin Historic Route 66" sign across from the Art Institute of Chicago, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend."

5 US DESTINATIONS NAMED TO BEST OF WORLD TRAVEL LIST FOR 2027 BY NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC

Before hitting the open road, travelers can grab breakfast at Lou Mitchell's, an old-style diner long known as a traditional first stop for motorists, AARP noted.

Visitors can also walk along Jackson Boulevard, which formed part of the original route, or take in views of the city from Skydeck Chicago, according to the outlet.

Heading southwest into Missouri brings travelers to Springfield, widely known as the "Birthplace of Route 66."

Officials met in the city in 1926 and proposed the name "U.S. Route 66" for the highway linking Chicago to Los Angeles, AARP noted.

FOX NEWS' STEVE DOOCY TRAVELS ROUTE 66, UNCOVERS THE STORIES THAT BUILT AMERICA OVER A CENTURY

Today, visitors can browse shops along historic Commercial Street, explore the Wonders of Wildlife National Museum & Aquarium or catch a movie at the restored Gillioz Theatre, a 1926 theater that hosted live shows during the route's early years, according to the guide.

Farther down the road, Oklahoma's capital sits near the middle of the route and showcases Western history and art at the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend."

Travelers can also stroll through the 15-acre Myriad Botanical Gardens or explore the shops and restaurants in the Bricktown Historic District, AARP noted.

Those staying overnight can book a room at the Skirvin Hotel, a landmark property that has welcomed guests since 1911, according to the outlet.

Continuing west into the Texas Panhandle, smaller towns show what Route 66 looked like before major interstates took over.

In Vega, which was bypassed when Interstate 40 was built, travelers can visit Dot's Mini Museum one block off the old highway, Fox News Digital previously reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The free museum stays unlocked so visitors can browse 20th-century antiques, and Dot's granddaughter, Keila Bain, told Fox News her late grandmother inspired a character in the Disney-Pixar movie "Cars."

"Our town was bypassed by I-40, but you know, there are a lot of people who travel, who love to go into the town, meet the people, see the places," Bain said.

Just 15 minutes west of Vega sits Adrian, recognized as the geographical midpoint of Route 66, according to Gary Daggett, president of the Old Route 66 Association of Texas.

"It's the nostalgia, ya know. There's so much of American history here at Route 66," Daggett told Fox News Digital.

While in town, drivers can stop at the Midpoint Café, which owner Brenda Hammit Bradley said is known for its homemade pies and inspired Flo's V8 Café in "Cars."

Crossing into New Mexico, Albuquerque has the longest surviving city stretch of original Route 66, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend."

Eighteen miles of neon signs, retro motels and vintage storefronts line Central Avenue, leading visitors from historic Old Town to the art galleries and music venues of Nob Hill, AARP noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Travelers can also ride the Sandia Peak Tramway or spend the night at Hotel Parq Central, a restored building that once served as a railroad hospital, according to the outlet.

Heading into eastern Arizona, Route 66 passes near the Painted Desert, where old-school roadside attractions still draw passing drivers, Fox News Digital reported.

One popular photo stop along that stretch is a large dinosaur model near the highway that dates back to midcentury family road trips.

Farther west in Arizona sits Winslow, a desert town immortalized in The Eagles' hit song "Take It Easy," Fox News Digital noted.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

That musical tie has turned Winslow into a lasting stop for music fans and road-trippers looking to visit a piece of American pop culture.

Flagstaff is one of the best-preserved Route 66 towns and long served as a mountain stop for travelers heading west, according to AARP.

Visitors can stop by the Flagstaff Visitor Center and Historic Train Depot to learn how Americans shifted from train travel to road trips in 1926, the outlet said.

Travelers can also shop for Native American jewelry or visit the Museum Club, a former log cabin that now hosts country music acts, according to the guide.

After more than 2,400 miles on the road, travelers reach the Pacific Ocean at the Santa Monica Pier, celebrated as the "End of the Trail" for Route 66.

Visitors can take a photo next to the historic "End of the Trail" sign, ride the pier's solar-powered Ferris wheel or walk along Ocean Avenue to mark the end of the trip, AARP noted.

Fox News Digital's Gary Gastelu and Chelsea Torres contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump says it would be 'hard' to work with Chuck Schumer: 'He will fail again'
item.description: President Donald Trump says it will be "hard" to work with Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, claiming the Democratic leader will "fail again."
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump predicted it would be "hard" to work with Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., if he is chosen to continue leading Senate Democrats next year.

Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday that Schumer is likely to "fail again" if he is elected. Schumer is running for Senate majority leader once again, but opposition to his leadership is gaining steam.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader. He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again," Trump wrote.

DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

"All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. Here we go again!" he added.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Schumer's main challenger is Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who represents a more radical wing of the party. His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats; Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races.

SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., also threw her support behind Van Hollen last week.

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting.

The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," and that he has "the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."

Fox News' Hanna Panreck contributed to this report.

item.title: Transgender doctor accused of pursuing relationship with patient barred from practicing medicine
item.description: Transgender doctor Dr. Jemstone Bathe is no longer practicing medicine in Manitoba following claims the physician pursued a sexual relationship with a patient.
item.content:encoded:
A transgender doctor who provided transgender transition assistance in Canada has been barred from practicing medicine after allegedly pursuing a sexual relationship with a patient, including exchanging explicit messages and discussing prescription hormones in a sexual context, according to local reporting.

Dr. Jemstone Bathe, who previously practiced medicine in Wisconsin, is no longer practicing, effective Nov. 16, according to a notice on Bathe's profile via a website search for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba. The restrictions prohibit Bathe from practicing medicine in any jurisdiction, including through online platforms, until receiving express permission from the College's Investigation Committee or its chair.

Bathe’s profile on the website for The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba reads in part, "Dr. Bathe will not resume the practice of medicine until such time as Dr. Bathe has the express permission of the Investigation Committee or the Chair of the Investigation Committee (the "Chair") to do so."

DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS

It continues, "Dr. Bathe will not hold themselves out to any person as practicing medicine (as described in paragraph 4), whether in person or online, and Dr. Bathe will not practice medicine in any jurisdiction or forum."

The Winnipeg Free Press reported Tuesday that a former patient of Bathe's told the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba that Bathe had pursued a sexual relationship with them.

The patient, who identifies as transgender and uses they/them pronouns, was unnamed so as to not disclose their identity and was quoted as saying, "I was just scared to be myself. I lost who I was. It destroyed me."

The patient said Bathe began trying to have a sexual relationship almost immediately after the patient’s first medical appointment at Klinic in early March, according to the Winnipeg Free Press.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Wendy Elias-Gagnon, director of communications for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba, said, "Confidentiality requirements in our provincial legislation, the Regulated Health Professions Act (RHPA), limit what we can disclose about physicians. We cannot provide details beyond what is in their public profile."

MICHIGAN HOSPITAL PAYS $410K TO SETTLE LAWSUIT BY PHYSICIAN ASSISTANT FIRED OVER TRANSGENDER POLICY

Elias-Gagnon added that people can access publicly available details for Manitoba physicians at the college’s profile search.

On Bathe’s LinkedIn profile, Bathe identifies as a "Gender Affirming Care Physician."

The profile says Bathe "started in medicine as an EMS-Explorer at age 15 with Edwardsburg Ambulance Service. After undergrad in Kalamazoo, Michigan, she went to medical school in Detroit at Wayne State University School of Medicine, followed by a residency in Internal Medicine at the Detroit Medical Center. She finished her residency during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, moving to practice as an attending hospitalist with Marshfield Medical Center."

PLANNED PARENTHOOD OFFERED HORMONES BUT HAD NO ANSWERS WHEN DETRANSITIONER SOUGHT HELP, UNDERCOVER PROBE FINDS

According to the social media page, Bathe transitioned from acute care to primary care in 2021 in an effort to safeguard mental health. Bathe subsequently pursued her current path in medicine after experiencing what Bathe described as severe transphobia and professional challenges while practicing in rural Wisconsin.

Bathe, according to the LinkedIn summary, received little support while working in Rice Lake, Wisconsin, and said the Trump administration's return to power threatened the physician’s ability to continue practicing medicine in the United States, as well as her access to medical care and personal safety.

It concludes, "Thanks to her wonderful partner, Paula (she/her), Jemstone sought out assistance from MLA Logan Oxenham. He then put her in touch with Manitoba Physician Retention and Recruitment as well as Klinic Community Health. Unfortunately, things at Klinic were not meant to be. We all get better together. And we all deserve to be happy as our best selves. That includes you."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Bathe for comment.
